#7875. Are Dogs the Secret to a Happier, Healthier Childhood?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Dogs have been a fixture of family life for thousands of years, and many people who grew up with one say they canât picture their childhood without them. Beyond the obvious benefits of companionship and fun, growing up with a dog has been shown to have positive effects on physical and emotional well-being; advantages that show up in how children handle friendships, feelings, and everyday challenges.

Of course, this doesnât mean that having a dog is right for everyone. Bringing a dog into your home is a big decision that affects budgets and daily routines for years to come, and the best outcomes tend to come from families who go in with open eyes.

For anyone considering life with a dog, here are a few ways they can improve a childâs life, and things to consider before adopting one.

Growing up around animals can lower the chance of developing allergies later on. Dogs, and all the things that come with living with them, expose children to a range of allergens, which helps build a more robust immune system. The key seems to be early exposure, which means the sooner a dog becomes part of a childâs world, the better.

Children who are close to their dogs tend to be more securely attached to their parents, and theyâre more likely to form strong friendships, too. Strong relationships in one part of a childâs life seem to go hand in hand with strong relationships in others. Kids who share more physical contact with their dogs, from cuddles to roughhousing, tend to get along better with their moms, dads, and friends.

Kids who grow up with a family dog tend to have lower rates of anxiety. The benefits reach well beyond childhood, too. Dogs can ease feelings of depression and anxiety in adults who went through childhood trauma, and they can reduce signs of post-traumatic stress, which is part of the reason theyâre so often brought into therapy.

A dog is a living, breathing creature with needs, and children who help care for one learn responsibility and dependability. A five-year-old canât take on every chore, but age-appropriate tasks are a great place to start. Young children spend much of their lives at the mercy of parents and teachers, so having a dog to look after can give them a real sense of empowerment and build self-esteem.

Caring for an animal from an early age also builds empathy, which supports emotional intelligence and helps a child grow into a more compassionate person. The lessons go on from there. Dogs model loyalty; training and bonding teach patience, and learning to read a dogâs body language and respect their boundaries teaches respect. When a family pet eventually passes away, children also learn about death and grieving.

Children with pets tend to have better self-esteem than children without them. The effect appears to be strongest as kids approach adolescence; an age when the emotional support of a companion animal may matter most.

Families with dogs tend to be more physically active than their peers, getting about 11 extra minutes of exercise a day. That may not sound like much, but it adds up to roughly 5.5 hours a month in a society that is growing more sedentary all the time.

For some children, the effect is far larger. Girls in particular gained around 52 minutes of light physical activity a day after a dog joined the family. The flip side was striking too, since girls who lost their pet saw their daily activity drop by 62 minutes.

Children tend to handle stressful moments better with a dog nearby. They feel happier and more at ease, and being able to touch the dog calms them even further. Simply having a furry companion close by seems to help kids feel steadier inside.

For all the upsides, adopting a dog isnât a decision to take lightly, and there are a few things every family needs to consider before racing out to get a four-legged friend.

Budget: Dogs depend on their owners for food, veterinary care, and emergencies, and a household budget that canât cover those costs is a reason to rethink the plan.

Age: Although many childhood benefits increase the earlier they start living with a dog, sometimes waiting until children are older is a good idea. St. Bernards make fantastic family pets, for example, but they can weigh as much as 180 pounds and can hurt a child accidentally. Small breeds have their own risks, since they can be fragile and prone to injury until kids learn boundaries and how to respect animals.

Lifestyle: A family that works long hours and spends every evening shuttling children to activities needs a plan for what the dog will be doing. Not every schedule has room for a pet, and that is perfectly fine, but a dog shouldnât be adopted without free time to spend with it.

Motivation: Children often beg for a dog, promising to walk, feed, and pick up after them.

Then, the novelty fades, and the adults end up with the bulk of the care. Although itâs a good idea to encourage children to take on some of the responsibility of looking after a dog, you should assume that youâll be the one doing most of the work â hope for the best, plan for the worst!

Growing up alongside a dog can bring real benefits, from fewer allergies and lower anxiety to stronger relationships and more time spent moving. But to enjoy the benefits of living with a dog, families need to have the time, money, and genuine desire to take care of one.

Growing up with a dog might not guarantee health and happiness, but itâs a pretty good place to start!

Now the heat’s on in your home, dry air means many houseplants are struggling to stay healthy. A homemade pebble tray is the no-cost solution that brings larger, lusher leaves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Many leafy plants we now grow as houseplants evolved in hot and humid rainforests which is why, now fall’s here and the heat’s turned on, the dry air in our homes is leading to less-than-lovely foliage. So, if you're wondering how to keep houseplants healthy in winter so you can enjoy lush, glossy leaves, you're not alone. Thankfully, a humidity tray is the quick and easy DIY solution that will speed your houseplants back to happy in time for the holidays, and it won't cost you a dime.

It’s a cruel fact that it’s the plants with the biggest or boldest leaves that struggle most in the dry air of our winter-heated homes: adapting to life in a rainforest is exactly why the foliage is so fabulous in the first place. Beneath a dense forest canopy, sunlight is a precious commodity so some plants like Elephant Ear (Alocasia) grow huge leaves to catch as much light as possible. Others such as peace lilies has foliage densely packed with chlorophyll to absorb as much of the scarce light as possible, and that's what creates their intense, deep green hue. Some like Calathea have purple or red undersides to their leaves precisely so that precious light gets bounced back into the leaf.

So, if you want to enjoy these dramatic leaves at their best, you have to provide these houseplants with the humidity level they need to flourish. Any plant likely suffering from a lack of humidity at this time of the year is easy to spot, starting with any houseplants with brown leaf tips or edges, smaller or discolored leaves, or slow growth. Now, to restore these ailing houseplants to lush, glossy growth, you could treat them to a small humidifier like the Homedics Humidifier from Amazon. Or you could simply DIY a humidity tray with stuff you’ve probably already got in your backyard.

A humidity tray, also called a pebble tray, is a shallow container that’s wider than the plant pot it serves, filled with small pebbles and water. The plant pot sits on the pebbles above the water level so instead of water being pulled up into the potting soil, it evaporates into the air. The higher the heat in your home, and so the drier the air, the more water evaporates to create a humid microclimate around your houseplant.

An old plant saucer is perfect, or if you’d like something more decorative for your houseplant display, look in your kitchen cupboards for a deep plate or shallow dish. Fill this with fine gravel or small pebbles – pea gravel is perfect and you can buy bagged pea gravel pebbles from Home Depot very cheaply if you don’t have a gravel path or driveway to raid.

Then simply stand the plant pot on top of your DIY humidity tray and keep the water topped up, making sure the water level stays below the base of the pot.

Grouping your houseplants together will also help to raise the humidity. Clustering plants together creates an indoor microclimate because the water vapor that’s lost through the leaves diffuses more slowly – and this effect is amplified if even one or two of the grouped houseplants have humidity trays.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Houseplants that have evolved to live in the damp environments of rainforests and woodland are most sensitive to humidity. These common houseplants all thrive in 55-80% humidity and will benefit from a DIY pebble tray:

If you grow any of these houseplants, then a $5 room thermometer like this from Amazon that measures humidity levels as well as temperature, and records the minimum and maximum levels in the past 24 hours, is a really useful tool. You’ll be able to see exactly what the humidity levels are and, if they’re too low, take action before the plant tells you it’s an issue with brown leaf tips. Already made the plant a pebble tray? To raise the humidity further, simply DIY a wider one to increase the surface area of water available to evaporate.

Many more adaptable houseplants won’t be as dramatic about a less-than-ideal humidity level, but add a little more moisture to the air and they’ll grow faster and produce bigger leaves with a better color and shine. Making a DIY pebble tray will help all these plants to flourish:

These plants all thrive in humidity levels of 40-60%. While that's likely within the average humidity of a home in summer, it's a different story in winter. Because cold air can't hold as much water, and home heating dries it further, home moisture levels typically drop to 20-40%. While that lack of humidity isn't enough to kill these adaptable plants, it will certainly prevent them from looking their best.

Leaves with brown tips and outer edges are the most common sign that a houseplant is struggling in low humidity levels and is losing moisture from its foliage faster than the roots can replace it. All plants release water vapor from tiny pores on their leaves and, in dry air, that moisture is sucked out at a faster rate. The plant parts furthest away from the roots supplying the water are the first to run out of moisture, which is why leaf tips are the first to dry out to a crispy brown. At this time of the year, it's very common to see houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants with brown leaf tips. Low humidity is also an easily-avoided reason why peace lily flowers turn brown.

There are other symptoms to look out for too, such as slow growth and smaller new leaves. While many plants naturally produce aerial roots, if you spot a sudden escalation in their number, the houseplant is likely seeking more humidity. And if you find that the potting soil dries out super-quickly after watering, too-dry air may be the cause.

Misting houseplants provide a quick fix but the spike in humidity only lasts for a very short time, whereas a humidity tray delivers constant moisture to create a more permanent microclimate. To match the humidity levels provided by a pebble tray, you’d need to mist houseplants every hour, every day, every night. Misting can also create a breeding ground for fungal and bacterial disease by leaving water sitting on foliage.

In dry or arid zones like Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico or Colorado, your houseplants may need humidity trays topped up year-round. You’ll likely see even plants that don’t require very high air moisture levels developing brown tips, which is a sure sign that they’ll benefit from a humidity tray.

At the other end of the scale, if you live in a high-humidity climate like Louisiana, Mississippi or Florida, only the houseplants that are highly dependent on humidity need a pebble tray – unless your home is equipped with an efficient air-conditioning system that dehumidifies, and dependant on your winter home-heat level, of course. Unnecessary standing water in a warm, damp home puts plants at a higher risk of pests and fungal disease.

Gifting many of your houseplants a DIY humidity tray will help them to flourish in our heated homes through fall and winter, and happy plants grow leaves that are larger and lusher, greener and glossier. Along with a cheap thermometer that displays air moisture percentages, your DIY pebble tray makes it very easy to adjust humidity levels, too. Keep the trays topped up with water for maximum humidity, and gradually reduce if needs be once your home's heat is turned off. You can even leave the trays water-free over summer if natural humidity is high enough in your climate, and let your DIY pebble saucers serve as stylish houseplant decor for a personal touch, until the heat's turned back on.

#7873. War Dogs of History: Sergeant Stubby and the Birth of the American War Dog Legend

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

Stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in New Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

When the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

After surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

Stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

During the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

Conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

Stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a new generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

Stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Morgan Farr is a writer, graphic designer, and advocate who has spent her career telling the stories of working dogs and the people who love them. She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument. She previously served as the social media manager for the U.S. Army Military Working Dog Program.

Together with her husband, an Army veterinarian, Morgan co-founded Canine Advancement Group, which offers education on canine wellness and welfare for both working and companion dogs. She is a member of the American Veterinary Medical History Society, the American Historical Association, the American Association for State and Local History, and the Society for Military History. In 2025, she was named the Armed Forces Insurance Military Spouse of the Year for Joint Base San Antonio.

#7872. President Trump's Defamation Claim Against BBC Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From today's decision by Judge Jeffrey Kuntz (S.D. Fla.) in Trump v. BBC:

In Trump v. CNN (S.D. Fla. 2023), aff'd (11th Cir. 2025), Judge Singhal concluded that "the complained of statements are opinion, not factually false statements, and therefore are not actionable." In Trump v. Dow Jones & Co., Inc. (S.D. Fla. 2026), Judge Gayles dismissed President Trump's claims that the Wall Street Journal failed to adequately investigate claims it reported.

Those cases involved a news entity reporting on a story. Here, the news entity created the story. BBC admitted as much by confirming it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made.

And it acknowledged it chose to release the video in a documentary only a week before the 2024 Presidential Election, at the time it would have the most impact. To make sure it was seen in Florida, BBC even emailed U.S. and Florida based commenters with instructions to on how to view the documentary.

Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day. For now, after careful review, and being otherwise fully advised, BBC's Motion to Dismiss is denied [as to the defamation claim] ….

On October 28, 2024, one week before the 2024 Presidential Election, BBC broadcast a documentary titled "Trump: A Second Chance." In the Documentary, a twelve-second segment portrayed President Trump giving a speech to his supporters on January 6, 2021:

We're going to walk down to the Capitol and I'll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell and if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore.

This two sentence, twelve-second segment, represents the core of Trump's complaint. However, the issue with the statement is that Trump never said it. The above statement is actually two parts of a speech spliced together. Instead, the first remarks that Trump made were:

Now it is up to Congress to confront this egregious assault on our democracy. And after this, we're going to walk down and I'll be there with you. We're going to walk down, we're going to walk down. Anyone you want but I think right here, we're going to walk down to the Capitol and we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them.

Nearly fifty-five minutes later, Trump continued:

[B]ut I said 'Something's wrong here, Something's really wrong, can't have happened.' And we fight, we fight like hell, and if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore.

Additionally, less than a minute later, Trump told his supporters to peacefully walk to the Capitol, stating:

I know that everyone here will soon be marching over to the Capitol building to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard[.]

It is those two statements, edited and spliced together, that form the alleged defamatory twelve-second segment that aired in the Documentary. BBC admits Trump never made the statements as aired. The Chairman of BBC apologized to Trump, stating that the BBC "editing unintentionally created the impression of a single continuous section of your speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech." This, the BBC chairman stated, "gave the mistaken impression that you had made a direct call for violent action. That was an editorial error and it should not have happened." …

The court concluded that President Trump had adequately alleged actual damages and "actual malice" (i.e., knowing and reckless falsehood) on BBC's part, though of course the court noted that both would still have to be proved eventually as a factual matter. An excerpt:

For purposes of the defamation test, ill-will is different from actual malice. An intention to portray a public figure in a negative light, even when motivated by ill-will or evil intent, is not sufficient to show actual malice unless the publisher intended to inflict harm through knowing or reckless falsehood. However, ill-will or motive, when combined with other evidence, may be taken into account for actual malice….

Here, Trump alleges that BBC has a history of unfair or improper coverage toward him. In addition to the Documentary itself, Trump highlights the Prescott Memorandum, a 2022 BBC Newsnight episode, and the "2024 BBC News Shooting Hoax." As an important reminder, the state of mind required for actual malice must be "brought home" to the person in the BBC's organization responsible for the publication of the Documentary. This principle is relevant as it relates to the 2022 Newsnight episode and the 2024 "Shooting Hoax." Again, Trump has not alleged that either of these incidents involved the creator(s) of the Documentary. That said, these incidents are not merely portrayal in a negative light, but examples of BBC playing fast and loose with the factual accuracy of their media content. With respect to the Newsnight episode, the BBC seemingly did not care about the falsity of the portrayal until the later Documentary became an issue. Such examples can be said to be probative of BBC's state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC's non-action toward false statements about Trump.

Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump. BBC asks the Court to put on blinders and treat the Panorama team as if they were blocked off from the rest of the organization, ignorant of everything else going on at BBC. At this procedural stage [i.e., a motion to dismiss, where plaintiff must merely plausibly allege facts that could lead to liability, rather than proving them -EV], the Court simply cannot ignore the circumstantial evidence presented. To do so would make it extremely difficult to ever prove a defendant's subjective state of mind in any defamation case….

Trump alleged that BBC's editing of the speech was an "intentional and malicious effort to falsely and deceptively portray President Trump as having called for violence." In support, Trump alleges that it "would have been impossible for BBC's journalists and producers to splice together two distinct parts of the [s]peech from nearly fifty-five minutes apart unless they were acting intentionally." On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice. BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.

Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the Documentary.

In addition to the editing itself, BBC's Chairman issued an apology:

The way the speech was edited in the documentary gave a misleading impression of what you said. The editing unintentionally created the impression of a single continuous section of your speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech. This gave the mistaken impression that you had made a direct call for violent action. That was an editorial error and it should not have happened.

However, the BBC now appears to disagree with the apology issued by the Chairman. BBC's Chairman admitted that the documentary gave a misleading and mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action. Strangely enough, BBC strays from that position in the Motion to Dismiss, referring to statements made by January 6 defendants as evidence that the speech may be interpreted as a call to violent action. But BBC's own Chairman acknowledged the editing was misleading in his letter to Trump….

As a final matter on the issue of actual malice, Trump alleges that BBC strayed from accepted standards of journalistic integrity. Such a claim on its own would not amount to actual malice, since actual malice requires "more than a departure from reasonable journalistic standards." A failure to investigate, standing on its own, does not indicate the presence of actual malice. To show actual malice, there must be some showing that the BBC purposefully avoided further investigation with the intent to avoid the truth.

BBC first argues that allegations BBC failed to contact Trump for comment before publishing are insufficient to establish actual malice. On this point, the Court agrees.

BBC then argues that allegations that BBC omitted portions of Trump's speech are also insufficient to establish actual malice. Alterations of quotes that "materially alter" the meaning of Trump's statements could support a finding of actual malice…. BBC did not just alter the quote but created a new quote by splicing two statements together and passing them off as a single continuous sentence. To the extent that there was no material alteration to the meaning of Trump's speech, that simply cannot be the case. The Chairman's letter makes it very clear that BBC acknowledges there was a material change of meaning when they edited the speech to create a single continuous segment that did not exist.

BBC then argues that the apology "militates against a finding of actual malice." … Today, retractions can be issued near instantaneously for online publications thanks to the internet. The Court acknowledges that media entities, like The Washington Post, or BBC, are not perfect, and make mistakes. However, it cannot be said that a retraction the next day is in the same ballpark as a retraction over a year later, and only after being threatened with legal action. The temporal distance here makes the retraction a weak indicator as to BBC's state of mind at the time of publication.

Further weakening BBC's argument, BBC was aware that such editing created a false impression as early as 2022. Former Acting White House Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney, in relation to the 2022 Newsnight episode, stated on-air: "Your video actually spliced together the presentation.… [Y]our video makes it look like those two things came together." As BBC's own Clive Coleman stated "[t]he first lesson … you're taught as a broadcast journalist is that you do not joint two bits of footage together from different times in a way that will make the audience think that it is one piece of footage." Considering these facts, BBC's ultimate retraction in 2025 reads less like a readiness to retract, and more like a reluctance to retract.

The Court acknowledges that events from 2022 do not directly bear on the state of mind at the time of publication. But neither does a retraction over a year after publication. Hence why courts are often reliant on circumstantial evidence when making state of mind determinations. Still, Trump's allegations regarding BBC's departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence….

Of course, all of this does not prove BBC acted with actual malice. But it does make it plausible. And Trump need only allege facts sufficient to give rise to a reasonable inference that the BBC edited and published the Documentary "with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." Trump has done so here….

And the court held the BBC's statement could be viewed as a false factual allegation, rather than merely "convey[ing] an opinion of what the audience understood Trump to say":

As Trump correctly points out, a spliced segment that creates a sentence that Trump never spoke represents the exact kind of false statement of fact that courts hold as the sine qua non for recovery in defamation. Whether the audience "reasonably interpreted" the segment to convey that Trump called for violence is irrelevant….

The court also held that Florida courts (including the federal courts) had jurisdiction over the BBC. But the court rejected Trump's Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act claim:

… FDUTPA is limited to acts "in the conduct of any trade or commerce." The statute defines this as "the advertising, soliciting, providing, offering, or distributing" of goods, services, property, "or any other article, commodity, or thing of value." … "[M]agazines and newspapers often have commercial purposes, but those purposes do not convert the individual articles within these editorial sources into commercial speech." Both advertising and subscriptions are typical features of newspapers, whether online or in-print. Even if BBC has commercial purposes, that does not convert the Documentary into commercial speech….

Alejandro Brito, Ian Michael Corp, Jalaine Garcia, and Michael O. Mena (Brito, PLLC), Daniel Epstein (Epstein & Co.), Edward Andrew Paltzik (Tylor Dykema) represent Trump.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Ever wondered if those used coffee grounds could be helping your houseplants? If you’re looking for a few ready-made pick-me-ups, here’s what you can give your indoor plants

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every household generates a mass of organic kitchen waste, from morning coffee grounds to evening fish bones. Quite often, thanks to social media and online forums, we’ll hear about some novel way to use key scraps to help plants. These quirky DIY tricks can seem so compelling and easy (and also free) that it’s tempting to toss scraps straight into the potting soil around your plants.

A few kitchen scraps can help a little, and some can actually help with fertilizing houseplants, once they're prepared the right way. But that last bit is important. You need to make sure you are using the right kind of scraps, and that you have prepared them so they can be absorbed or processed well. Fail to do this, and there’s a chance that helpful impulse could result in fuzzy mold and tiny gnats.

The kitchen scraps I’ve rounded up here can help to supply trace minerals, organic matter, and subtle soil-structuring benefits to your potted greenery. These scraps all need prep first, though, whether that's drying, grinding or some time in a compost pile or worm bin. If you want to unlock their gentle benefits, this is a good time to get things moving. Houseplants slow down as the days get shorter, so they don't need much extra food until spring – giving you time to turn some trash into treasure.

When it comes to the best scraps for houseplants, preparation and application are key. Never dump wet, chunky food scraps onto the soil surface, as they can trap stagnant moisture and invite houseplant pests. Instead, use one of these preparation methods: air or oven-drying, grinding into fine powder, brewing, or indoor composting with a worm bin.

Indoor composting bins don’t require lots of knowledge or experience these days, and you can pick up units that make composting a highly beneficial background activity. If you’re interested in a compact unit for indoors, the Original VermiHut System, available from Amazon, is a neat and super-easy way to turn scraps into rich, houseplant-safe worm castings. Once your scrap of choice has been treated, you can gently work small amounts into the top inch (2.5cm) of potting mix.

Prioritize pot hygiene with any scraps you do try out. Check that every container has unobstructed drainage holes and keep a close eye on treated pots for 2-3 weeks. If you spot any white fuzz, scrape it off and allow the top layer to dry. Remember that kitchen scraps are meant to be gentle supplemental boosters, not replacements for quality potting soil and a balanced seasonal feeding routine. Here are 6 scraps you can safely try with your houseplants – plus, which scraps to leave in the bin.

The buzz around coffee grounds for houseplants is mostly about nitrogen (along with trace potassium and magnesium). That nitrogen is tied up in organic matter, though, and soil microbes will need to break it down before the roots can use it. Select plain, unflavored Arabica or Robusta grounds, and avoid flavored coffees containing synthetic oils, syrups, or spices.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Never spread damp grounds thickly over indoor soil, as they can mold and dry into a crust that repels water. Instead, spread used grounds on a baking sheet to dry, then blend a small handful (no more than 5-10% of total volume) into a fresh potting mix, or process through an indoor worm bin first. Contrary to myth, brewed grounds will not reliably acidify your potting soil, as brewing pulls a good share of the acid into your cup. For a good potting mix, buy Espoma Organic Potting Mix from Walmart.

Eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate, and plants need calcium to strengthen cell walls and support healthy new leaf development. But don’t toss large shell fragments into a houseplant pot. Calcium carbonate dissolves at a glacial pace, especially in neutral or alkaline potting mixes. Instead, rinse away the egg white, let shells air-dry for 48 hours, and pulverize them into a fine powder.

For grinding, use a dedicated grinder, a pestle and mortar, or a processor like the Cuisinart Mini Food Processor from Amazon, which is compact and super-fast. For a faster mineral release, soak the shell powder in a splash of mild lemon juice or vinegar for 24 hours. The mild acid reacts with the calcium carbonate to create plant-available calcium citrate. Just remember to dilute before applying. Work a light pinch into potting soil once or twice a year, skipping acid-loving plants like African violets, as the calcium can gradually raise soil pH.

Banana peels (along with closely related plantain peels) are rich in potassium, which regulates water uptake and boosts flowering. They also contain trace phosphorus and magnesium. However, burying chunks of raw banana or plantain peel in your houseplant’s potting soil is a really bad idea. Dense, sugary peels rot sluggishly in pots, attracting fruit flies and encouraging root-rotting pathogens.

Chop banana (or plantain) peels into small pieces and process in a compost bin or worm farm until crumbly, before blending into potting mix. Alternatively, dehydrate clean peels in a low oven until crispy, grind them into a powder, and sprinkle a spoonful into the soil. While soaking peels in water for 48 hours creates a mild banana tea, it leaches only trace nutrients. If you’re looking for targeted liquid feeds, you’re better off with a balanced fertilizer such as Espoma’s Organic Indoor 2-2-2 Plant Food, available from Walmart, and adding it during spring and summer growth.

Plain, steeped tea leaves offer gentle organic matter, trace nitrogen, and mild tannic acids that subtly condition soil structure and improve moisture retention. However, you need to stick to unflavored black, green, white, or pure herbal teas like chamomile or rooibos. And make sure they are steeped without milk, sugar, or honey. Avoid heavily spiced chai blends or artificially flavored teas, as the essential oils can irritate delicate root hairs.

Tear open used tea bags and discard the pouch, as most tea bags contain plastic fibers. Never pile wet leaves on top of the soil, as they can encourage gnats and mold. Instead, spread the loose leaves on a paper towel until dry and lightly fork a teaspoon into the topsoil, or drop them into a worm bin. Used gently once a month in spring and summer, they give moisture-loving tropicals like ferns, calatheas, and pothos a gentle lift. If you don’t have any compost going, Home Depot carries Noble Worm Organics Worm Castings, and a little of that does the same job.

Pungent alliums like onions and garlic, spicy peppers, or fibrous potato skins should never be buried straight into pots. They can ferment and summon fungus gnats. However, you can safely capture minerals by making a liquid tonic from key vegetable scraps. Save the cooled, unsalted water left over from boiling or steaming nutrient-dense vegetables like carrots, potatoes, broccoli, or leafy greens. Use this mineral-rich water at room temperature instead of watering once or twice a month, discarding any leftovers after 24 hours so bacteria cannot multiply.

Alternatively, you can route clean trimmings through an indoor worm bin. Bury solid scraps like carrot peelings, lettuce cores, and squash trimmings beneath damp bedding in a compact indoor worm bin. In 8-12 weeks, red wigglers can convert them into odorless vermicompost. You can buy Uncle Jim’s Worm Farm Live Red Wigglers from Amazon for hardworking composting worms to transform carrot peels and used greens into nutrient-rich castings. Then add to plants, applying 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per quart (0.95 L) of potting mix around the base, and water in.

Rinsing uncooked white, brown, or jasmine rice leaves behind cloudy, starch-rich water containing trace amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) along with B vitamins. While scientific evidence shows its direct fertilizer value is modest and varies widely by grain type, those gentle starches can act as a mild prebiotic snack for beneficial soil microbes in healthy potting mixes. However, use only fresh, unsalted and unseasoned rinse water (or cooled, unsalted boiling water).

Apply it the same day in place of a standard watering once a month. Never store rice water in jars to ferment. DIY fermented rice water quickly breeds foul-smelling bacteria. Likewise, avoid salted pasta water. While plain starchy pasta water is harmless, even a pinch of cooking salt accumulates in closed pots and can quickly reach a level where it scorches roots. If you’re after a good indoor watering can, choose something with a gooseneck spout that can target the base of the plant, such as the Megawodar Copper Watering Can from Amazon.

Even with careful prep, certain kitchen leftovers need to be kept far away from your indoor garden. Meat, fish, and dairy products are the big ones. Oily and greasy foods are also non-starters. Animal proteins and fats rot rapidly in warm indoor temperatures, creating unbearable odors, attracting flies, and coating soil particles in a waterproof film that suffocates roots.

Salty and sugary leftovers are equally destructive. Salted pasta water, soup broths, and seasoned cooking liquids leave behind sodium deposits that build up in closed pots, drawing moisture out of roots and leaving foliage with crispy brown leaf tips. Meanwhile, sugary sauces, fruit juices, and citrus rinds trigger fungal growth and attract household ants.

When monitoring your houseplants in the weeks after adding your kitchen scraps, keep a close eye out for fuzzy molds and fungus gnats. Used early, you can add sticky traps like LightsMax Dual-Sided Yellow Sticky Traps from The Home Depot to manage adult gnats and other flying pests.

By drying, grinding, or brewing, or letting an indoor worm bin do the heavy lifting first, you can enrich your potting mix sustainably and give your houseplants a gentle helping hand with ingredients destined for the trash.

Backyard birds tapping on windows is a sometimes funny, sometimes infuriating part of fall. Here's why they do it, and how to stop the behaviour if needs be.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile. Now research and observations from bird experts have revealed the real reasons behind this bizarre behaviour, and you may be surprised to learn what they are.

Some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one. Avian experts, however, have put forward reasons based on cold, hard data, and they provide a fascinating insight into fall bird behaviour.

Whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall. Understanding the likely causes will also help you decide if should take action to stop the window tapping to save birds from harm, and save your sanity, too.

As temperatures decrease in fall, insects become more scarce, many birds are forced to forage for food in new areas. Because glass retains heat from the sun as well as windows allowing some of a home’s heat to escape, any tiny gaps in frames become welcoming nooks for insects to enter diapause (similar to hibernation) – and consequently, one of those spots hungry birds may favor. You might think modern windows don’t offer much space for critters to hole up in, but those drainage weep holes and sliding tracks provide plenty of opportunities. Spiders also use window corners to spin insect-catching webs and lay eggs, offering further protein-rich food to the bird buffet.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO), there’s a rise in birds pecking at windows for food in fall and winter, and in particular by the tit family which includes chickadees and titmice. The organisation also cites that birds may pick at traditional window putty as it’s made with fish or linseed oil, both a valuable source of energy in colder months.

Research carried out by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology found that the lower angle of sunlight hitting windows in fall significantly increases how reflective the glass is. Aside from birds having no concept of what a window is, our feathered friends see differently to us. Most birds have eyes on the sides of their heads to give them almost-360° vision, and while that’s highly useful for spotting potential predators, it means their forward vision isn’t as good as ours. So, reflections in windows are easily interpreted as extra habitat and when birds encounter the glass – which in fall, especially, can appear to them as an invisible barrier – they may peck at it repeatedly to investigate.

Fall is when juvenile birds disperse, and these inexperienced youngsters have a lot to learn about the world around them, and much spatial awareness still to develop. Data published by the American Bird Conservancy and the US Fish & Wildlife Service shows a strong rise in what they term ‘glass interactions’ in fall. While many of these will be window collisions caused by mirror-like glass and navigational error, some will be window pecking led by curiosity as birds investigate their surroundings.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While territorial behaviour among most of our feathered friends peaks in spring, many resident birds claim their territory in fall, according to the National Audubon Society. Northern cardinals, non-migrating American robins, northern mockingbirds, towhees and bluebirds are all highly territorial through fall into winter. And there's a very good reason for this, because as summer broods disperse, thousands of juvenile birds search a new territory. In the face of this competition, existing populations fiercely defend their established territories – especially if it contains a valuable food source such as a garden shrub hung with berries birds love through winter!

With windows becoming mirror-like in the low fall sun, dominant birds can attack their own reflection, mistaking it for a competitor. So this is a common reason why birds tap windows in fall as well as spring.

Whether you have a towhee aggressively pecking at your patio doors or a chickadee tap-tapping your bedroom window at all hours, now you understand what’s behind this behaviour, you can do something about it. Gentle pecking for food harms neither bird nor human, so it’s safe to ignore this low-level behaviour. But more insistent pecking at a window, fighting imagined aggressors or attempting to break through an invisible barrier is not just highly annoying to us but harmful to birds, damaging beaks and wasting valuable energy.

Taking action to stop birds pecking windows involves making glass more visible, or keeping birds away from it in the first place. That means these solutions will also reduce the risk of feathered friends flying into windows and injuring themselves. By working out the likely reason behind a bird tapping on your window, you can choose the method that will be most effective.

Your first step to stop birds tapping windows is to move any houseplants away from windows that are being targeted. To a young bird, a windowsill full of greenery can look like inviting habitat or contribute to the illusion that this could be a continuation of their flightpath.

A quick and cheap solution if the targeted window opens is to shut a length of double-sided reflective bird scare tape like this from Amazon in it. When the tape blows in the wind, its holographic surface casts erratic patterns of ultraviolet light which most birds perceive as a threat. For resident birds in search of tasty insects, this may be enough for them to deem that window an unsafe zone.

While the go-to for making windows more visible to birds and preventing collisions is decals, they're only effective if the gaps between them are narrow enough. A few decals dotted about on a large window are next to useless as birds will likely perceive the areas between them as possible flightpaths, just as they do the gaps between branches in woodland.

A far simpler, more effective and still-stylish alternative is to create a grid of dots around 2 inches apart across the entire window. Use a white oil-based permanent marker like a Sharpie Medium Point Paint Marker, available from Amazon, and for a professional result, use a stencil template. You could make your own by punching holes in cardboard or save yourself the trouble with an Avi-Dot Bird Saver Window Stencil from Etsy.

Another effective way to help birds see house windows as a barrier is to stick on clear collision tape like CollidEscape, available from Amazon. To be effective against bird strikes, and therefore cut down on curious birds pecking at what they perceive as an invisible wall, you’ll need to position the tape in vertical or horizontal stripes with the edges no more than 2 inches apart. If you have feathered friends that often peck at a particular part of a window, this is a useful method as you can reduce the gap between strips here.

If a particular bird still persists in pecking at a window, creating a temporary cardboard barrier can help break the habit.

If you have a problem with a particularly territorial or bigger bird such as a woodpecker or seagull, a final resort is to fix a permanent deterrent near to the targeted window. Wind-powered metal spinners throw out unpredictable flashes of light, visually confusing birds to create an area they perceive as unsafe. Windmill spinners like these Stainless Steel Bird Deterrent Devices by Ebern Designs on Wayfair mean you don’t have to compromise on garden style.

Backyard birds need our support more than ever once fall turns to winter, whether that's preventing a bird bath freezing over to preserve their water supply, saving up kitchen scraps to feed feathered friends, or making sure smaller songbirds get a fair share of food. Now you understand why birds tap on windows in fall, you can decide whether or not to ignore the behaviour or take action for your and the bird's benefit.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.
